tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). cited.words: (a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due.

(a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) .

(b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2).

(2) In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due. The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons. Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon. If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required. Public housing tenants or tenants receiving rent subsidies are required to deposit only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible pursuant to the federal, state, or local program in which they are participating.

answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, but the law doesn't settle it. A landlord can end a lease with no chance to fix the problem only for certain violations. One of those is a "subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance." You describe one night of noise, with no earlier warning. That is a weak fit, and you can argue the landlord should have given you a chance to fix it first. The landlord can argue that a disturbance after midnight is serious enough to skip that step. Your landlord has not filed an eviction case, so this letter is not a court order. The notice counts 7 days from May 4, which ends May 11, and that date has not passed. Has there been any other night of loud noise or any other complaint from neighbors, besides May 1?

DETAILS

### What kind of notice did you get?
- By your account, the letter says your lease "is terminated effective immediately" and gives you 7 days from delivery to leave. It blames loud music after midnight on May 1.
- That is the "no chance to fix it" kind of notice. It is described in Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a).
- The other kind gives you 7 days to correct the problem before the lease ends. It is described in 83.56(2)(b). Your letter does not offer that.
- The manager handed you the letter at the door on May 4. Hand delivery is a valid way to deliver this kind of notice (83.56(4)).

### Can the landlord skip the chance to fix the problem?
- Section 83.56(2)(a) allows an immediate termination notice in two situations.
  - The first is when the violation is "of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it." The statute's examples are intentional damage to property, fraudulent entry, and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance."
  - The second is when the violation happens again "within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation."
- The second situation does not fit. You told me there was no earlier warning, written or spoken.
- The first situation is the open question. The law does not settle it, so here are both readings.
  - **Landlord's reading:** Loud music after midnight is an "unreasonable disturbance," and your lease sets quiet hours of "10:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m." (lease section 11). Under this reading, the landlord could end the lease without a chance to fix it.
  - **Your reading:** The statute's example says "subsequent or continued" disturbance, meaning it happened before or keeps happening. One night with no prior warning is neither. The statute's examples for violations you get a chance to fix include breaking the lease through unauthorized guests, pets, or parking (83.56(2)(b)). A one-time party looks more like those. Under this reading, the landlord needed to give you 7 days to correct it and sent the wrong notice.
- Whether other nights of noise happened matters here. It could move this toward the landlord's reading.

### What does the lease say?
- Section 11 of the lease requires you and your guests to "keep noise at a level that does not disturb other residents."
- The lease does not say a first violation ends the tenancy.
- The lease also cannot take away your rights under the notice rules. Under 83.56(4), "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement."

### What deadline does the letter set, and what happens next?
- The 7 days to vacate run from the delivery date, May 4, and end May 11. That date has not passed. This counts calendar days and does not shift for weekends or holidays. That counting method has not been checked against the statute.
- No eviction case has been filed. If one is filed, you would raise the argument above as a defense in that case.
- To defend an eviction for breaking the lease, you must comply with 83.60(2), which involves the court registry (83.56(5)(b)). If you don't, the court must enter a default judgment for removal (83.56(5)(b)).
- If the landlord accepts rent from you knowing about the noise, the landlord gives up the right to end the lease over that violation. That does not cover a later or continuing violation (83.56(5)(a)).

tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant has received a landlord's written notice about a lease violation other than unpaid rent (the 7-day notice). There are two kinds. One gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The other says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. It covers fixing the problem, defending an eviction case over the notice, and the landlord giving up the right to end the lease by accepting rent. It does not decide which kind of notice the landlord should have sent, or whether the one sent is valid. A demand for unpaid rent is a different situation; load notice_received_nonpayment for it.

The statute leaves some housing out of this part: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)) This matters when the tenant lives in college housing. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies to the tenant's housing. Say that it could matter and that the tool does not decide it.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, from the notice in their hands. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; you apply the term to their answer.

### From the lease (search_lease)

- The lease clause or rule the notice points to: read it and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did.
- The notices clause: where the tenant's reply must be sent. A lease clause about notices does not change the notice rules: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)) Give that sentence next to such a clause.
- What the lease requires when a tenant moves out, if the notice says the lease is terminated.

### From the tenant

- The date the landlord's notice was delivered to them (not the date it was written), and how it reached them: handed to them, mailed, e-mailed, left at the door, or something else.
- What the notice says they did. Ask them to copy the words from the notice.
- Whether the notice gives them 7 days to fix the problem, saying the lease will end if they do not.
- Whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives them 7 days to move out.
- Whether, before this notice, the landlord had ever given them a written warning or notice about anything. If so, the date they got it and what it was about.
- Whether they have fixed the problem the notice describes, and on what date.
- Whether the landlord has accepted rent from them since the notice was delivered.
- Whether the landlord has filed an eviction case in court against them. If so, whether they have paid the rent the court papers claim into the court registry, or filed a motion asking the court to decide the amount.

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes a deadline (see Deadlines) only from facts the tenant has confirmed: the date the notice was delivered, whether the notice gives 7 days to fix the problem, and whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. Only one of the two deadlines applies, depending on the kind of notice. When the tenant tells you one of these, propose it for their record, so they can confirm it.

### Evidence worth keeping

- The notice itself, with a photo of where it was left, or the envelope or the e-mail headers.
- Photos or other proof of the correction, with dates.
- Any earlier written warning.
- Receipts for rent paid after the notice.
- The lease clause or rule the notice points to.

## What the tenant can do

Before any step, say whether the tenant can do it, what that turns on, and what is left to do. Each condition below is settled in one of four ways. The lease can settle it: read that clause with search_lease and say what it says. The tenant can tell you. It is not settled: give the open question from the section below. Or it is outside the tool: say what to check and where.

### Fix the problem the notice names within 7 days

Fixing it means the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. Two conditions need to be met.

1. The notice gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The statute describes it: "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether the notice gives that chance. If it says the lease ends at once, this option is not open on this notice; say so.
2. The 7 days after delivery have not ended, or the problem was fixed within them: "within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether the 7 days have ended comes only from the program's deadlines. If the tenant says they fixed the problem, ask for the date, and set it beside the last day of the 7 days the program shows. The tool compares no dates, so say that and let the tenant see it.

The step: the problem the notice names is fixed. The statute's form of this notice says: "Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether it is fixed. Two open questions apply: delivered or received, and the 12 months.

### Defend an eviction case on the ground that the notice ended the lease without the chance to fix

This is for a notice that ended the lease at once over a violation the statute says should have had a chance to be fixed. Four conditions need to be met.

1. The notice ends the lease with no chance to fix the problem. The statute's form for it says: "You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) The tenant tells you whether their notice says that.
2. The violation is of a nature the tenant should be given a chance to fix: "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This is not settled for a violation like neither list's examples; give the open question on which paragraph applies.
3. There was no written warning of a similar violation in the 12 months before: "if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). The tenant tells you whether there was an earlier warning. If there was, set the date of the earlier warning and what it was about beside this notice. The tool does not count months.
4. The landlord has filed an eviction case: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b)) If the tenant says no case has been filed, say a defense is raised in a case once one is filed.

The step: the rent is paid into the registry of the court, as the statute requires of a tenant who defends ("must comply with s. 83.60 (2)" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b))). The tenant tells you whether they did. Section 83.60 is not loaded with this skill; fetch it before you describe what it requires. The open question on the 12 months applies.

### The landlord gave up ending the lease by accepting rent knowing of the violation

Two conditions need to be met. There are no steps for the tenant to take.

1. The landlord accepted rent after knowing of the violation: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The tenant tells you whether the landlord has accepted rent since the notice.
2. The violation did not go on after the rent was accepted, nor happen again: "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Ask whether the problem the notice names stopped before the rent was accepted and has not happened again.

The full sentence: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a))

## Deadlines

The program computes two deadlines, both the tenant's, both counted from the date the landlord's notice was delivered (not the date it was written), once the tenant has confirmed that date. Only one applies.

- Seven days to fix the problem. It counts only when the notice gives the chance to fix. The statute: "deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)) The statute then adds: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b))
- Seven days to vacate. It counts only when the notice says the lease is terminated. The statute: "In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a))

The program computes and prints every date. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself, not even for 'what if it ran from another day'. Whether a period has passed comes only from the program's deadlines (get_deadlines). The program prints the counting convention with each date: calendar days, the delivery day not counted, no weekend or holiday adjustment. It is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against these statutory deadlines. If the tenant asks how the days are counted, say so. The tool counts days only and does not compute a 12-month period.

## What the statute does not settle

For each question below, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading with what it would mean for them, and pick none. Where one step works under every reading, say so.

- Which paragraph applies. 83.56(2)(a) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), with examples: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). 83.56(2)(b) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), with examples such as "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant's notice shows which kind the landlord sent; set the violation it describes beside each list. What stays open is a violation like neither list's examples, sent as a notice that ends the tenancy at once.
  - The landlord's notice stands when the violation is like 83.56(2)(a)'s examples, or repeats within 12 months of a written warning of a similar violation.
  - A violation like 83.56(2)(b)'s examples must get the notice with 7 days to correct, and a notice under 83.56(2)(a) for it denies the tenant the chance the statute says the tenant 'should be given'.
- Delivered or received. The text of 83.56(2)(b) runs the period "from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), while the model form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tool counts from the delivery date the tenant gives. When delivery and receipt are the same day the question does not arise.
  - The statute's own words govern: 7 days from the date the written notice is delivered.
  - The form the statute prescribes tells the tenant 'within 7 days of receipt', and a tenant who relies on it should not lose by the difference.
- The 12 months. Both paragraphs refer to a period of 12 months: a "written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), and noncompliance that "recurs within 12 months after notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This tool counts in days and does not compute a 12-month period. Set the dates the tenant gives beside the words and say the tool does not count the months.

## Letters

Every letter needs: today's date, the notice and its date, the tenant's account or the correction made, and how the tenant will deliver it. The tenant sends the letter; you send nothing. Read the lease's notices clause with search_lease and tell the tenant where and how the lease says the reply must be sent.

The postures, each with its own line:

- preserve: States the tenant's account and any correction made, and asks the landlord to confirm the matter is resolved. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.56(2)(b) sentence, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.56(5)(a) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant this. The 7-day periods the program computes run from the date the landlord's notice was delivered, as they gave it. 83.56(2)(b) speaks of a noncompliance "corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). A letter from them does not change that date. What the statute looks to is whether the noncompliance was corrected within the period, and the letter can say when it was.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Counting from the date the notice was written instead of the date it was delivered.
- Saying the tenant must leave in 7 days when the notice offers a chance to correct, or that correcting the violation ends the matter when the notice ends the tenancy at once.
- Saying the violation was corrected in time without the tenant's correction date beside the 7-day date the program shows. The tool compares no dates.
- Saying the landlord may terminate, or that the tenant failed to cure, on a notice that offers a chance to correct while its 7 days have not run. The landlord terminates only "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether that period has passed comes from the program's deadlines.
- Skipping 83.56(5)(a). A landlord who "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)) waives the right to terminate for it, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)).
- Computing a 12-month period. The tool counts days only.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 23, ch. 82-66; s. 6, ch. 83-151; s. 14, ch. 83-217; s. 6, ch. 87-195; s. 6, ch. 93-255; s. 6, ch. 94-170; s. 1373, ch. 95-147; s. 5, ch. 99-6; s. 8, ch. 2013-136; s. 5, ch. 2025-16; s. 2, ch. 2026-143.

answer:
**Short answer:** Not automatically. The notice says to leave within 7 days, but it doesn't make you leave. No eviction case has been filed, and only a court can order you out. Your notice also looks weak. It ends your lease at once with no chance to fix the problem, and the law lists "unauthorized guests" as a problem a tenant should usually get a chance to fix. The law doesn't say for certain which kind of notice your landlord had to send. Your boyfriend has moved out, so the problem has stopped. Under the program's count, the 7 days run through April 13, 2026. Since you had no earlier warning, you have a real argument that the notice doesn't hold. Even so, a court would decide that, not you or the landlord.

Has your landlord taken any payment from you since the notice was handed to you on April 6?

DETAILS

### Does the notice make you leave in 7 days?
- The notice follows the wording the law gives for a notice that ends a lease at once. Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a) says the tenant "shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises."
- If you don't leave, the landlord has to file an eviction case. You've confirmed none has been filed.
- The program counts 7 days from April 6, the day the manager handed you the notice. That gives April 13, 2026. It counts calendar days, doesn't count the start day, and makes no weekend or holiday adjustment. That counting method hasn't been checked against the statute.
- Passing April 13 doesn't mean you're automatically out. It means the landlord could then file a case.

### Was this the right kind of notice?
The law has two kinds of notice for a lease violation that isn't unpaid rent.
- **Notice that ends the lease at once.** Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a) allows it when the violation is "of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it." It also allows it for a repeat violation "within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation." Its examples are intentional damage to property and repeated unreasonable disturbance.
- **Notice with 7 days to fix the problem.** Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b) covers a violation "of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it." Its examples include "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles."

Here is how your facts fit each reading:
- **Your reading:** An overnight guest is the kind of problem listed in (2)(b). You had no warning, so the landlord should have given you 7 days to fix it. A notice that ends the lease at once denies you that chance.
- **The landlord's likely reading:** The guest rule is a lease term you broke. The landlord may say the violation was serious enough that you didn't need a chance to fix it.
- The statute doesn't settle which reading is right. The guest example in (2)(b) is on your side. A court would have to decide.

### What does the lease say?
- Section 11 of your lease says: "A guest may stay no more than 14 nights in any six months without Landlord's written consent." The notice points to this rule. You've confirmed your boyfriend stayed more than 14 nights.
- Section 8 says notices to you are delivered to the apartment. The manager handed it to you at the door. The law allows delivery by "delivering a true copy thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)), so the way it was delivered doesn't look like the problem.
- A lease can't change the notice rules. Fla. Stat. 83.56(4) says: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement."

### Does the earlier-warning question matter?
- You had no earlier warning, written or spoken. The "repeat violation" route in (2)(a) needs a written warning within the prior 12 months. On your facts, that route isn't open to the landlord.
- The tool doesn't count months. It matters only if a written warning turns up.

### Does your April rent help you?
- You paid April rent on April 1, before the notice. Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a) says a landlord who "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance" gives up the right to end the lease for that violation.
- Your payment came before the notice. Whether the landlord knew about your boyfriend's stays on April 1 isn't something I know.
- Any payment the landlord takes after April 6 could matter more. That's why I asked.

### What happens if the landlord files a case?
- You would have to pay rent into the court registry to raise a defense, such as that the notice was the wrong kind. Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b) says a tenant who defends "must comply with s. 83.60 (2)."
- Under 83.60(2), you must pay the accrued rent claimed in the case, plus rent that comes due while it's pending. Or you must file a motion to set the amount. You have 5 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after being served.
- If you miss that deadline, you give up your defenses. The landlord then gets an immediate default judgment for removal, with a writ of possession to issue without a hearing.
- No case has been filed, so none of this applies yet.

### What should you keep?
- Keep the notice itself.
- Keep proof of the April 1 rent payment.
- Keep any proof of the date your boyfriend moved out.
- Keep any later receipts for rent.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant has received a landlord's written notice about a lease violation other than unpaid rent (the 7-day notice). There are two kinds. One gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The other says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. It covers fixing the problem, defending an eviction case over the notice, and the landlord giving up the right to end the lease by accepting rent. It does not decide which kind of notice the landlord should have sent, or whether the one sent is valid. A demand for unpaid rent is a different situation; load notice_received_nonpayment for it.

The statute leaves some housing out of this part: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)) This matters when the tenant lives in college housing. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies to the tenant's housing. Say that it could matter and that the tool does not decide it.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, from the notice in their hands. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; you apply the term to their answer.

### From the lease (search_lease)

- The lease clause or rule the notice points to: read it and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did.
- The notices clause: where the tenant's reply must be sent. A lease clause about notices does not change the notice rules: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)) Give that sentence next to such a clause.
- What the lease requires when a tenant moves out, if the notice says the lease is terminated.

### From the tenant

- The date the landlord's notice was delivered to them (not the date it was written), and how it reached them: handed to them, mailed, e-mailed, left at the door, or something else.
- What the notice says they did. Ask them to copy the words from the notice.
- Whether the notice gives them 7 days to fix the problem, saying the lease will end if they do not.
- Whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives them 7 days to move out.
- Whether, before this notice, the landlord had ever given them a written warning or notice about anything. If so, the date they got it and what it was about.
- Whether they have fixed the problem the notice describes, and on what date.
- Whether the landlord has accepted rent from them since the notice was delivered.
- Whether the landlord has filed an eviction case in court against them. If so, whether they have paid the rent the court papers claim into the court registry, or filed a motion asking the court to decide the amount.

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes a deadline (see Deadlines) only from facts the tenant has confirmed: the date the notice was delivered, whether the notice gives 7 days to fix the problem, and whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. Only one of the two deadlines applies, depending on the kind of notice. When the tenant tells you one of these, propose it for their record, so they can confirm it.

### Evidence worth keeping

- The notice itself, with a photo of where it was left, or the envelope or the e-mail headers.
- Photos or other proof of the correction, with dates.
- Any earlier written warning.
- Receipts for rent paid after the notice.
- The lease clause or rule the notice points to.

## What the tenant can do

Before any step, say whether the tenant can do it, what that turns on, and what is left to do. Each condition below is settled in one of four ways. The lease can settle it: read that clause with search_lease and say what it says. The tenant can tell you. It is not settled: give the open question from the section below. Or it is outside the tool: say what to check and where.

### Fix the problem the notice names within 7 days

Fixing it means the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. Two conditions need to be met.

1. The notice gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The statute describes it: "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether the notice gives that chance. If it says the lease ends at once, this option is not open on this notice; say so.
2. The 7 days after delivery have not ended, or the problem was fixed within them: "within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether the 7 days have ended comes only from the program's deadlines. If the tenant says they fixed the problem, ask for the date, and set it beside the last day of the 7 days the program shows. The tool compares no dates, so say that and let the tenant see it.

The step: the problem the notice names is fixed. The statute's form of this notice says: "Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether it is fixed. Two open questions apply: delivered or received, and the 12 months.

### Defend an eviction case on the ground that the notice ended the lease without the chance to fix

This is for a notice that ended the lease at once over a violation the statute says should have had a chance to be fixed. Four conditions need to be met.

1. The notice ends the lease with no chance to fix the problem. The statute's form for it says: "You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) The tenant tells you whether their notice says that.
2. The violation is of a nature the tenant should be given a chance to fix: "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This is not settled for a violation like neither list's examples; give the open question on which paragraph applies.
3. There was no written warning of a similar violation in the 12 months before: "if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). The tenant tells you whether there was an earlier warning. If there was, set the date of the earlier warning and what it was about beside this notice. The tool does not count months.
4. The landlord has filed an eviction case: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b)) If the tenant says no case has been filed, say a defense is raised in a case once one is filed.

The step: the rent is paid into the registry of the court, as the statute requires of a tenant who defends ("must comply with s. 83.60 (2)" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b))). The tenant tells you whether they did. Section 83.60 is not loaded with this skill; fetch it before you describe what it requires. The open question on the 12 months applies.

### The landlord gave up ending the lease by accepting rent knowing of the violation

Two conditions need to be met. There are no steps for the tenant to take.

1. The landlord accepted rent after knowing of the violation: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The tenant tells you whether the landlord has accepted rent since the notice.
2. The violation did not go on after the rent was accepted, nor happen again: "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Ask whether the problem the notice names stopped before the rent was accepted and has not happened again.

The full sentence: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a))

## Deadlines

The program computes two deadlines, both the tenant's, both counted from the date the landlord's notice was delivered (not the date it was written), once the tenant has confirmed that date. Only one applies.

- Seven days to fix the problem. It counts only when the notice gives the chance to fix. The statute: "deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)) The statute then adds: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b))
- Seven days to vacate. It counts only when the notice says the lease is terminated. The statute: "In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a))

The program computes and prints every date. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself, not even for 'what if it ran from another day'. Whether a period has passed comes only from the program's deadlines (get_deadlines). The program prints the counting convention with each date: calendar days, the delivery day not counted, no weekend or holiday adjustment. It is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against these statutory deadlines. If the tenant asks how the days are counted, say so. The tool counts days only and does not compute a 12-month period.

## What the statute does not settle

For each question below, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading with what it would mean for them, and pick none. Where one step works under every reading, say so.

- Which paragraph applies. 83.56(2)(a) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), with examples: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). 83.56(2)(b) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), with examples such as "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant's notice shows which kind the landlord sent; set the violation it describes beside each list. What stays open is a violation like neither list's examples, sent as a notice that ends the tenancy at once.
  - The landlord's notice stands when the violation is like 83.56(2)(a)'s examples, or repeats within 12 months of a written warning of a similar violation.
  - A violation like 83.56(2)(b)'s examples must get the notice with 7 days to correct, and a notice under 83.56(2)(a) for it denies the tenant the chance the statute says the tenant 'should be given'.
- Delivered or received. The text of 83.56(2)(b) runs the period "from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), while the model form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tool counts from the delivery date the tenant gives. When delivery and receipt are the same day the question does not arise.
  - The statute's own words govern: 7 days from the date the written notice is delivered.
  - The form the statute prescribes tells the tenant 'within 7 days of receipt', and a tenant who relies on it should not lose by the difference.
- The 12 months. Both paragraphs refer to a period of 12 months: a "written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), and noncompliance that "recurs within 12 months after notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This tool counts in days and does not compute a 12-month period. Set the dates the tenant gives beside the words and say the tool does not count the months.

## Letters

Every letter needs: today's date, the notice and its date, the tenant's account or the correction made, and how the tenant will deliver it. The tenant sends the letter; you send nothing. Read the lease's notices clause with search_lease and tell the tenant where and how the lease says the reply must be sent.

The postures, each with its own line:

- preserve: States the tenant's account and any correction made, and asks the landlord to confirm the matter is resolved. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.56(2)(b) sentence, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.56(5)(a) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant this. The 7-day periods the program computes run from the date the landlord's notice was delivered, as they gave it. 83.56(2)(b) speaks of a noncompliance "corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). A letter from them does not change that date. What the statute looks to is whether the noncompliance was corrected within the period, and the letter can say when it was.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Counting from the date the notice was written instead of the date it was delivered.
- Saying the tenant must leave in 7 days when the notice offers a chance to correct, or that correcting the violation ends the matter when the notice ends the tenancy at once.
- Saying the violation was corrected in time without the tenant's correction date beside the 7-day date the program shows. The tool compares no dates.
- Saying the landlord may terminate, or that the tenant failed to cure, on a notice that offers a chance to correct while its 7 days have not run. The landlord terminates only "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether that period has passed comes from the program's deadlines.
- Skipping 83.56(5)(a). A landlord who "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)) waives the right to terminate for it, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)).
- Computing a 12-month period. The tool counts days only.
- Computing any date yourself.

answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to move out right now. Your notice gives you a chance to fix the problem first. The 7 days run from March 9, the day the manager handed you the notice, not from March 2, the date on the letter. Counting from March 9, the last day is March 16, and that date hasn't passed. If the dog problem is fixed by then, your landlord can't end the lease based on this notice. If it isn't fixed, the landlord can treat the lease as ended and start an eviction case. Only a court can order you out, and no case has been filed.

What does "fixed" mean for you? Is the dog still in the apartment, and do you plan to rehome it or ask the office for written consent?

DETAILS

### Does the notice give you a chance to fix the problem?
- Yes. Your notice says you must "remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated." That follows the form in Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b), which covers problems the tenant "should be given an opportunity to cure."
- The statute lists "having or permitting unauthorized pets" as an example of that kind of problem.
- You won't have to leave on day 7 if you fix the problem in that time. You would have to leave only if you don't fix it.

### Which date do the 7 days count from?
- The statute counts from "the date that the written notice is delivered" (83.56(2)(b)). You told me it was handed to you on March 9.
- The tool counts calendar days and doesn't count the day of delivery. It has not checked that method against the statute, so treat March 16 as a working date.
- The notice says "receipt." Here you received it the day it was delivered, so the two words give the same date.
- A notice may be delivered by "delivering a true copy thereof" (83.56(4)). Handing it to you counts as delivery.

### What does your lease say about the dog?
- Clause 11 says: "Tenant shall not keep any pet in the apartment without Landlord's written consent."
- If you don't have written consent, the notice matches the lease.
- Fixing the problem could mean the dog is no longer in the apartment. It could also mean you get the landlord's written consent. Clause 10 says changes to the lease must be in writing and signed.
- I can't tell you whether the landlord would accept a different fix. That is a question for the office.

### Did paying March rent help you?
- If a landlord "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance," the landlord gives up the right to end the lease for that problem (83.56(5)(a)). That rule does not cover a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- You paid March rent on March 1, before the notice. I don't know if the landlord knew about the dog then. If the landlord did know, that could help you. If not, it likely doesn't.
- The dog is probably still in the apartment, which would be a continuing problem. That would weaken this argument.
- Rent you pay after the notice is a separate question. Keep receipts for any rent you pay.

### What if the dog problem comes back?
- The notice warns that if "this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months," the landlord can end your tenancy without another chance to fix it. This matches 83.56(2)(b).
- The tool counts days, not months, so it can't compute that 12-month period.

### Where do you send a reply?
- Clause 7 says written notices to the landlord go by hand to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street, or by certified mail to that address.
- Clause 8 says the landlord's notices go to your apartment. The statute says the notice rules "may not be waived in the rental agreement" (83.56(4)), so a lease clause can't take away your rights under them.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant has received a landlord's written notice about a lease violation other than unpaid rent (the 7-day notice). There are two kinds. One gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The other says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. It covers fixing the problem, defending an eviction case over the notice, and the landlord giving up the right to end the lease by accepting rent. It does not decide which kind of notice the landlord should have sent, or whether the one sent is valid. A demand for unpaid rent is a different situation; load notice_received_nonpayment for it.

The statute leaves some housing out of this part: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)) This matters when the tenant lives in college housing. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies to the tenant's housing. Say that it could matter and that the tool does not decide it.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, from the notice in their hands. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; you apply the term to their answer.

### From the lease (search_lease)

- The lease clause or rule the notice points to: read it and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did.
- The notices clause: where the tenant's reply must be sent. A lease clause about notices does not change the notice rules: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)) Give that sentence next to such a clause.
- What the lease requires when a tenant moves out, if the notice says the lease is terminated.

### From the tenant

- The date the landlord's notice was delivered to them (not the date it was written), and how it reached them: handed to them, mailed, e-mailed, left at the door, or something else.
- What the notice says they did. Ask them to copy the words from the notice.
- Whether the notice gives them 7 days to fix the problem, saying the lease will end if they do not.
- Whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives them 7 days to move out.
- Whether, before this notice, the landlord had ever given them a written warning or notice about anything. If so, the date they got it and what it was about.
- Whether they have fixed the problem the notice describes, and on what date.
- Whether the landlord has accepted rent from them since the notice was delivered.
- Whether the landlord has filed an eviction case in court against them. If so, whether they have paid the rent the court papers claim into the court registry, or filed a motion asking the court to decide the amount.

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes a deadline (see Deadlines) only from facts the tenant has confirmed: the date the notice was delivered, whether the notice gives 7 days to fix the problem, and whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. Only one of the two deadlines applies, depending on the kind of notice. When the tenant tells you one of these, propose it for their record, so they can confirm it.

### Evidence worth keeping

- The notice itself, with a photo of where it was left, or the envelope or the e-mail headers.
- Photos or other proof of the correction, with dates.
- Any earlier written warning.
- Receipts for rent paid after the notice.
- The lease clause or rule the notice points to.

## What the tenant can do

Before any step, say whether the tenant can do it, what that turns on, and what is left to do. Each condition below is settled in one of four ways. The lease can settle it: read that clause with search_lease and say what it says. The tenant can tell you. It is not settled: give the open question from the section below. Or it is outside the tool: say what to check and where.

### Fix the problem the notice names within 7 days

Fixing it means the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. Two conditions need to be met.

1. The notice gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The statute describes it: "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether the notice gives that chance. If it says the lease ends at once, this option is not open on this notice; say so.
2. The 7 days after delivery have not ended, or the problem was fixed within them: "within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether the 7 days have ended comes only from the program's deadlines. If the tenant says they fixed the problem, ask for the date, and set it beside the last day of the 7 days the program shows. The tool compares no dates, so say that and let the tenant see it.

The step: the problem the notice names is fixed. The statute's form of this notice says: "Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether it is fixed. Two open questions apply: delivered or received, and the 12 months.

### Defend an eviction case on the ground that the notice ended the lease without the chance to fix

This is for a notice that ended the lease at once over a violation the statute says should have had a chance to be fixed. Four conditions need to be met.

1. The notice ends the lease with no chance to fix the problem. The statute's form for it says: "You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) The tenant tells you whether their notice says that.
2. The violation is of a nature the tenant should be given a chance to fix: "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This is not settled for a violation like neither list's examples; give the open question on which paragraph applies.
3. There was no written warning of a similar violation in the 12 months before: "if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). The tenant tells you whether there was an earlier warning. If there was, set the date of the earlier warning and what it was about beside this notice. The tool does not count months.
4. The landlord has filed an eviction case: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b)) If the tenant says no case has been filed, say a defense is raised in a case once one is filed.

The step: the rent is paid into the registry of the court, as the statute requires of a tenant who defends ("must comply with s. 83.60 (2)" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b))). The tenant tells you whether they did. Section 83.60 is not loaded with this skill; fetch it before you describe what it requires. The open question on the 12 months applies.

### The landlord gave up ending the lease by accepting rent knowing of the violation

Two conditions need to be met. There are no steps for the tenant to take.

1. The landlord accepted rent after knowing of the violation: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The tenant tells you whether the landlord has accepted rent since the notice.
2. The violation did not go on after the rent was accepted, nor happen again: "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Ask whether the problem the notice names stopped before the rent was accepted and has not happened again.

The full sentence: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a))

## Deadlines

The program computes two deadlines, both the tenant's, both counted from the date the landlord's notice was delivered (not the date it was written), once the tenant has confirmed that date. Only one applies.

- Seven days to fix the problem. It counts only when the notice gives the chance to fix. The statute: "deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)) The statute then adds: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b))
- Seven days to vacate. It counts only when the notice says the lease is terminated. The statute: "In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a))

The program computes and prints every date. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself, not even for 'what if it ran from another day'. Whether a period has passed comes only from the program's deadlines (get_deadlines). The program prints the counting convention with each date: calendar days, the delivery day not counted, no weekend or holiday adjustment. It is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against these statutory deadlines. If the tenant asks how the days are counted, say so. The tool counts days only and does not compute a 12-month period.

## What the statute does not settle

For each question below, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading with what it would mean for them, and pick none. Where one step works under every reading, say so.

- Which paragraph applies. 83.56(2)(a) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), with examples: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). 83.56(2)(b) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), with examples such as "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant's notice shows which kind the landlord sent; set the violation it describes beside each list. What stays open is a violation like neither list's examples, sent as a notice that ends the tenancy at once.
  - The landlord's notice stands when the violation is like 83.56(2)(a)'s examples, or repeats within 12 months of a written warning of a similar violation.
  - A violation like 83.56(2)(b)'s examples must get the notice with 7 days to correct, and a notice under 83.56(2)(a) for it denies the tenant the chance the statute says the tenant 'should be given'.
- Delivered or received. The text of 83.56(2)(b) runs the period "from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), while the model form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tool counts from the delivery date the tenant gives. When delivery and receipt are the same day the question does not arise.
  - The statute's own words govern: 7 days from the date the written notice is delivered.
  - The form the statute prescribes tells the tenant 'within 7 days of receipt', and a tenant who relies on it should not lose by the difference.
- The 12 months. Both paragraphs refer to a period of 12 months: a "written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), and noncompliance that "recurs within 12 months after notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This tool counts in days and does not compute a 12-month period. Set the dates the tenant gives beside the words and say the tool does not count the months.

## Letters

Every letter needs: today's date, the notice and its date, the tenant's account or the correction made, and how the tenant will deliver it. The tenant sends the letter; you send nothing. Read the lease's notices clause with search_lease and tell the tenant where and how the lease says the reply must be sent.

The postures, each with its own line:

- preserve: States the tenant's account and any correction made, and asks the landlord to confirm the matter is resolved. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.56(2)(b) sentence, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.56(5)(a) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant this. The 7-day periods the program computes run from the date the landlord's notice was delivered, as they gave it. 83.56(2)(b) speaks of a noncompliance "corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). A letter from them does not change that date. What the statute looks to is whether the noncompliance was corrected within the period, and the letter can say when it was.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Counting from the date the notice was written instead of the date it was delivered.
- Saying the tenant must leave in 7 days when the notice offers a chance to correct, or that correcting the violation ends the matter when the notice ends the tenancy at once.
- Saying the violation was corrected in time without the tenant's correction date beside the 7-day date the program shows. The tool compares no dates.
- Saying the landlord may terminate, or that the tenant failed to cure, on a notice that offers a chance to correct while its 7 days have not run. The landlord terminates only "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether that period has passed comes from the program's deadlines.
- Skipping 83.56(5)(a). A landlord who "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)) waives the right to terminate for it, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)).
- Computing a 12-month period. The tool counts days only.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable.
