answer:
You can't be sure you're done if you leave by June 8. Moving out by then does what the notice demands, but the law doesn't clearly say whether you still owe rent through July. Your lease has no early-termination fee or other charge for leaving early. You can ask for your deposit back, but your landlord can likely keep part of it for the door. To protect your deposit rights, give the office written notice of your move-out today, with an address where you can be reached.

- **Rent:** You paid June rent on June 1. The law doesn't settle what happens to rent after a landlord ends the lease over damage. Under one reading, the landlord ended the lease, so rent stops when you leave. Under the other, the landlord can still hold you to the rent for the rest of the lease, through July 31, either by re-renting the unit for your account or by waiting.
- **Deposit:** You paid $1,050. Your landlord can claim part of it for the door, but only by sending you a formal written notice in time. If the notice never comes in time, the landlord loses the right to keep any of it.

Have you given the office anything in writing about leaving yet, and did it include an address where you can be reached?

DETAILS

### Does moving out by June 8 satisfy the notice?
- The notice says your lease is "terminated effective immediately" and gives you "7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises." That matches the form in Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a), which the statute allows for "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord's or other tenants' property by intentional act."
- The notice was handed to you on June 1. The tool counts 7 days from delivery and gives June 8. It counts calendar days and skips the day of delivery. That counting method hasn't been checked against the statute.
- June 8 is the last day, so there is no spare day. You said you don't dispute the damage, so I haven't looked at whether the notice could be challenged.
- The landlord has not filed an eviction case, and you plan to leave before the 7 days run out.

### Do you still owe rent through July?
- Your lease runs to July 31, 2026 (lease section 3). The lease has no clause about leaving early or about a fee for it.
- A fee for leaving early is allowed only if you signed a separate addendum agreeing to it (83.595(4)). Your lease doesn't show one, so no fee applies.
- The law doesn't settle whether the rest of the rent is owed after the landlord ends the lease. I'm not leaning either way.
  - **Reading 1:** The landlord ended the lease under 83.56(2)(a), which says the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement." A terminated lease means no more rent after you leave.
  - **Reading 2:** Your damage was a breach, and you gave up the apartment. Section 83.595 then lets the landlord choose one of three things.
    - The landlord can treat the lease as ended and retake the unit, "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)).
    - The landlord can re-rent for your account and hold you liable for "the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting" (83.595(2)). Under that choice, the landlord must make a good-faith effort to re-rent.
    - The landlord can "stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (83.595(3)).
- The choice would be your landlord's. A written agreement signed by both of you, saying what you owe and that nothing more is owed, would settle it (lease section 10 requires changes to be in a signed writing).
- One more point is worth knowing. If the landlord took your June rent knowing about the May 25 damage, the law says the landlord "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement" for that damage (83.56(5)(a)). You paid before the notice arrived, and I don't know what the landlord knew when the rent was taken. You said you won't fight, so I'm only noting that this point exists.

### What notice must you give before you leave?
- A tenant who leaves before the lease ends "must give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (83.49(5)).
- Your lease has no different rule for leaving. Section 7 says to hand notices to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send them there by certified mail. Section 6 requires a forwarding address in writing.
- For a June 8 move-out, the tool counts back 7 days and gives June 1, which is today. Hand a short letter to the office today with your move-out date and your new mailing address. Keep a copy.
- If you miss this, the landlord is relieved of the duty to send the deposit-claim notice. But the law says this "does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it" (83.49(5)).

### What happens to your deposit?
- Your landlord holds $1,050 in a non-interest-bearing account (lease section 5), so no interest is owed.
- If the landlord claims part of the deposit, the landlord must send you written notice by certified mail to your last known mailing address, with the reason. That notice must go out within 30 days after the rental agreement ends (83.49(3)(a)). Notice by e-mail doesn't count. Your lease section 8 says you have not agreed to e-mail notices.
- The law doesn't settle which date ends the rental agreement when you leave before the lease end. The tool gives two dates.
  - Counted from your move-out on June 8, the 30 days end July 8.
  - Counted from the lease end date of July 31, they end August 30.
  - Neither date has passed.
- If no proper notice arrives in time, the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit," but "may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (83.49(3)(a)).
- If the landlord claims part of the deposit, you have 15 days after you receive the notice to object in writing. If you don't object, the landlord may deduct the claim and must send you the rest within 30 days of the notice date (83.49(3)(b)). Not objecting doesn't stop you from suing later for a refund.
- If the landlord makes no claim, the deposit is due back within 15 days after the rental agreement ends (83.49(3)(a)). Counted from June 8, that is June 23.
- Because you don't dispute the damage, expect a claim for the door. You can object to the amount.
- If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney fee (83.49(3)(c)).
- Lease section 5 says the deposit may not be used for the last month's rent. Don't treat it as rent.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded notice_received_violation. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant has received a landlord's written notice about a lease violation other than unpaid rent (the 7-day notice). There are two kinds. One gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The other says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. It covers fixing the problem, defending an eviction case over the notice, and the landlord giving up the right to end the lease by accepting rent. It does not decide which kind of notice the landlord should have sent, or whether the one sent is valid. A demand for unpaid rent is a different situation; load notice_received_nonpayment for it.

The statute leaves some housing out of this part: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)) This matters when the tenant lives in college housing. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies to the tenant's housing. Say that it could matter and that the tool does not decide it.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, from the notice in their hands. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; you apply the term to their answer.

### From the lease (search_lease)

- The lease clause or rule the notice points to: read it and set it beside what the notice says the tenant did.
- The notices clause: where the tenant's reply must be sent. A lease clause about notices does not change the notice rules: "The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)) Give that sentence next to such a clause.
- What the lease requires when a tenant moves out, if the notice says the lease is terminated.

### From the tenant

- The date the landlord's notice was delivered to them (not the date it was written), and how it reached them: handed to them, mailed, e-mailed, left at the door, or something else.
- What the notice says they did. Ask them to copy the words from the notice.
- Whether the notice gives them 7 days to fix the problem, saying the lease will end if they do not.
- Whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives them 7 days to move out.
- Whether, before this notice, the landlord had ever given them a written warning or notice about anything. If so, the date they got it and what it was about.
- Whether they have fixed the problem the notice describes, and on what date.
- Whether the landlord has accepted rent from them since the notice was delivered.
- Whether the landlord has filed an eviction case in court against them. If so, whether they have paid the rent the court papers claim into the court registry, or filed a motion asking the court to decide the amount.

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes a deadline (see Deadlines) only from facts the tenant has confirmed: the date the notice was delivered, whether the notice gives 7 days to fix the problem, and whether the notice says the lease is terminated and gives 7 days to move out. Only one of the two deadlines applies, depending on the kind of notice. When the tenant tells you one of these, propose it for their record, so they can confirm it.

### Evidence worth keeping

- The notice itself, with a photo of where it was left, or the envelope or the e-mail headers.
- Photos or other proof of the correction, with dates.
- Any earlier written warning.
- Receipts for rent paid after the notice.
- The lease clause or rule the notice points to.

## What the tenant can do

Before any step, say whether the tenant can do it, what that turns on, and what is left to do. Each condition below is settled in one of four ways. The lease can settle it: read that clause with search_lease and say what it says. The tenant can tell you. It is not settled: give the open question from the section below. Or it is outside the tool: say what to check and where.

### Fix the problem the notice names within 7 days

Fixing it means the landlord may not end the lease on this notice. Two conditions need to be met.

1. The notice gives the tenant 7 days to fix the problem. The statute describes it: "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether the notice gives that chance. If it says the lease ends at once, this option is not open on this notice; say so.
2. The 7 days after delivery have not ended, or the problem was fixed within them: "within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether the 7 days have ended comes only from the program's deadlines. If the tenant says they fixed the problem, ask for the date, and set it beside the last day of the 7 days the program shows. The tool compares no dates, so say that and let the tenant see it.

The step: the problem the notice names is fixed. The statute's form of this notice says: "Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant tells you whether it is fixed. Two open questions apply: delivered or received, and the 12 months.

### Defend an eviction case on the ground that the notice ended the lease without the chance to fix

This is for a notice that ended the lease at once over a violation the statute says should have had a chance to be fixed. Four conditions need to be met.

1. The notice ends the lease with no chance to fix the problem. The statute's form for it says: "You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) The tenant tells you whether their notice says that.
2. The violation is of a nature the tenant should be given a chance to fix: "If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This is not settled for a violation like neither list's examples; give the open question on which paragraph applies.
3. There was no written warning of a similar violation in the 12 months before: "if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). The tenant tells you whether there was an earlier warning. If there was, set the date of the earlier warning and what it was about beside this notice. The tool does not count months.
4. The landlord has filed an eviction case: "Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2)." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b)) If the tenant says no case has been filed, say a defense is raised in a case once one is filed.

The step: the rent is paid into the registry of the court, as the statute requires of a tenant who defends ("must comply with s. 83.60 (2)" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(b))). The tenant tells you whether they did. Section 83.60 is not loaded with this skill; fetch it before you describe what it requires. The open question on the 12 months applies.

### The landlord gave up ending the lease by accepting rent knowing of the violation

Two conditions need to be met. There are no steps for the tenant to take.

1. The landlord accepted rent after knowing of the violation: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The tenant tells you whether the landlord has accepted rent since the notice.
2. The violation did not go on after the rent was accepted, nor happen again: "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Ask whether the problem the notice names stopped before the rent was accepted and has not happened again.

The full sentence: "If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a))

## Deadlines

The program computes two deadlines, both the tenant's, both counted from the date the landlord's notice was delivered (not the date it was written), once the tenant has confirmed that date. Only one applies.

- Seven days to fix the problem. It counts only when the notice gives the chance to fix. The statute: "deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)) The statute then adds: "If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b))
- Seven days to vacate. It counts only when the notice says the lease is terminated. The statute: "In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a))

The program computes and prints every date. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself, not even for 'what if it ran from another day'. Whether a period has passed comes only from the program's deadlines (get_deadlines). The program prints the counting convention with each date: calendar days, the delivery day not counted, no weekend or holiday adjustment. It is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against these statutory deadlines. If the tenant asks how the days are counted, say so. The tool counts days only and does not compute a 12-month period.

## What the statute does not settle

For each question below, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading with what it would mean for them, and pick none. Where one step works under every reading, say so.

- Which paragraph applies. 83.56(2)(a) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), with examples: "destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)) and "a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)). 83.56(2)(b) covers noncompliance "of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), with examples such as "having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tenant's notice shows which kind the landlord sent; set the violation it describes beside each list. What stays open is a violation like neither list's examples, sent as a notice that ends the tenancy at once.
  - The landlord's notice stands when the violation is like 83.56(2)(a)'s examples, or repeats within 12 months of a written warning of a similar violation.
  - A violation like 83.56(2)(b)'s examples must get the notice with 7 days to correct, and a notice under 83.56(2)(a) for it denies the tenant the chance the statute says the tenant 'should be given'.
- Delivered or received. The text of 83.56(2)(b) runs the period "from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)), while the model form says "within 7 days of receipt of this notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). The tool counts from the delivery date the tenant gives. When delivery and receipt are the same day the question does not arise.
  - The statute's own words govern: 7 days from the date the written notice is delivered.
  - The form the statute prescribes tells the tenant 'within 7 days of receipt', and a tenant who relies on it should not lose by the difference.
- The 12 months. Both paragraphs refer to a period of 12 months: a "written warning by the landlord of a similar violation" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(a)), and noncompliance that "recurs within 12 months after notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). This tool counts in days and does not compute a 12-month period. Set the dates the tenant gives beside the words and say the tool does not count the months.

## Letters

Every letter needs: today's date, the notice and its date, the tenant's account or the correction made, and how the tenant will deliver it. The tenant sends the letter; you send nothing. Read the lease's notices clause with search_lease and tell the tenant where and how the lease says the reply must be sent.

The postures, each with its own line:

- preserve: States the tenant's account and any correction made, and asks the landlord to confirm the matter is resolved. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.56(2)(b) sentence, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.56(5)(a) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant this. The 7-day periods the program computes run from the date the landlord's notice was delivered, as they gave it. 83.56(2)(b) speaks of a noncompliance "corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). A letter from them does not change that date. What the statute looks to is whether the noncompliance was corrected within the period, and the letter can say when it was.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Counting from the date the notice was written instead of the date it was delivered.
- Saying the tenant must leave in 7 days when the notice offers a chance to correct, or that correcting the violation ends the matter when the notice ends the tenancy at once.
- Saying the violation was corrected in time without the tenant's correction date beside the 7-day date the program shows. The tool compares no dates.
- Saying the landlord may terminate, or that the tenant failed to cure, on a notice that offers a chance to correct while its 7 days have not run. The landlord terminates only "if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(2)(b)). Whether that period has passed comes from the program's deadlines.
- Skipping 83.56(5)(a). A landlord who "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)) waives the right to terminate for it, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)).
- Computing a 12-month period. The tool counts days only.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded wants_to_leave_early. Its instructions:

# Wants to leave early

Rests on 83.595 (what the landlord may do), 83.43 (what an early termination fee and a security deposit are), 83.49 (the 7-day notice, and interest), 83.682 and 83.64 (servicemembers, and retaliation), 83.63 (damage to the home), 83.512 (flooding), 83.46, 83.57, and 83.575 (no set end date, and staying on after one), 83.56 and 83.505 (how notices are delivered), 83.47 (void lease clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), and 83.59 and 83.67 (abandonment, and belongings left behind). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The landlord has failed to make a repair or keep a lease promise, and that is part of why they want out: load repair_not_made too. Its option 1 is a way to end the lease; do not repeat it here.
- The landlord sent a notice saying the tenant broke the lease: load notice_received_violation too. Its "Moving out" part says what is not settled about rent after a landlord ends the lease.
- The tenant has already moved out and asks about the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- The lease has no set end date (month to month, or no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable" (83.46(2))): leaving is not early. Written notice ends it, delivered a way 83.56(4) names, by the rent period (83.57(1) to (4)); for month to month "by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). The last day for that: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the month they plan to end on. A tenant who stayed on with the landlord's permission after a set term ended, and leaves without that notice: "the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not. The 7 days' notice below also applies to them. The options below do not.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any clause or addendum on ending the lease early or on what is owed for it; any notice before leaving; subletting or bringing in a replacement; and who else signed. Quote each clause and cite it. A box counts only if it is marked.

- A set charge for leaving early, whatever the lease calls it (a fee, a re-rental charge, losing the deposit): "“Early termination fee” means any charge, fee, or forfeiture that is provided for in a written rental agreement and is assessed to a tenant when a tenant elects to terminate the rental agreement, as provided in the agreement, and vacates a dwelling unit before the end of the rental agreement." (83.43(6)). If it is not that, it is liquidated damages, which the stored text does not define. Either way the name does not save it: 83.595(4) covers both, and it counts only if it meets option 5's conditions. The definition leaves out rent and charges through the end of the month the landlord retakes the home, charges for damage, and a deal to settle or buy out the lease (83.43(6)).
- Any other clause setting what happens on leaving early, such as all the remaining rent falling due at once: 83.595 lists no such choice. Whether the clause stands is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is void to the extent it "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)), or it is a charge that needs option 5's conditions, since the definition leaves out rent only through that month. The other: 83.595 says what the landlord may do after a tenant leaves and does not bar a term both sides agreed to.
- A clause on subletting or a replacement tenant: say what it says. The stored text does not speak to subletting; anything past the lease's words is outside this tool.
- Someone else signed and stays: the stored text does not say what happens when one of several tenants leaves. Say what the lease says about each signer's share of the rent.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- planned_move_out: the date they plan to move out. lease_end_date: the date the lease ends.
- reason: why they want to leave, in their words.
- leaving_notice_given: the date they gave the landlord a written notice that they are leaving, how it went, and whether it gave an address.
- early_addendum: only if the lease you hold does not show it, whether they signed a separate paper about a fee for leaving early, which box is marked, and the amount.
- Only if the reason points to one: orders (what the military orders say, and how far away), servicemember_notice_received (the date the landlord received the written notice), damage_date and what was damaged (and who or what caused it), flood_loss_date.

## How to answer

Give only the options the facts point to, and name the others in one line (military orders, damage to the home, flooding, a landlord who failed a duty), so the tenant can say if one fits. When the facts point to none of those, say that part II names no right to end a lease with a set end date just because the tenant wants to move. The tenant can move out, but moving out or giving notice does not by itself end the lease or stop the rent. What they owe then depends on options 4 to 6.

## Option 1: military orders

All of these must be met.

1. **A servicemember.** The term has "the same meaning as provided in s. 250.01" (83.43(15)), which is not stored; the tenant can say whether they are one.
2. **One of the listed grounds** (83.682(1)(a) to (f)). Ask what the orders say:
   - "required, pursuant to a permanent change of station orders, to move 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises" (83.682(1)(a));
   - "prematurely or involuntarily discharged or released from active duty or state active duty" (83.682(1)(b));
   - released from active duty after leasing while on active duty, with the home 35 miles or more from the home of record (83.682(1)(c));
   - "After entering into a rental agreement" (83.682(1)(d)), orders into government quarters, or becoming eligible for them and choosing to move there (83.682(1)(d));
   - "temporary duty orders, temporary change of station orders, or state active duty orders to an area 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises, provided such orders are for a period exceeding 60 days" (83.682(1)(e));
   - a change of orders to 35 miles or more away, before moving in (83.682(1)(f)).
   Orders or a move that fit none of these: not met. Say so in one sentence and go on to the other options.
3. **A written notice with proof.** "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (83.682(2)).
4. **The date.** The notice takes effect "on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (83.682(1)). The earliest date: count_days(servicemember_notice_received, 30). Before the landlord has it, the last day it must arrive to end the lease on the planned date: count_days(planned_move_out, -30).

What it gives: "the tenant is liable for the rent due under the rental agreement prorated to the effective date of the termination" (83.682(4)), and "The tenant is not liable for any other rent or damages due to the early termination of the tenancy as provided for in this section." (83.682(4)). Terminating 14 or more days before moving in: "no damages or penalties of any kind will be assessable." (83.682(4)). "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (83.682(5)). The landlord may not retaliate for it (83.64(1)(d)). Do not work out the prorated amount.

If the tenant also signed an addendum for a fee or liquidated damages, it is not owed; say so plainly. Ending the lease this way is a right, not a breach, and 83.595 opens "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement" (83.595). A fee is assessed when a tenant terminates "as provided in the agreement" (83.43(6)), and this termination is under the statute. Liquidated damages are damages, which (4) rules out. And no agreement can change this section (83.682(5)).

If the servicemember died on active duty, an adult in the immediate family may end the lease the same way, with the death certificate (83.682(3)).

## Option 2: the home was damaged

"If the premises are damaged or destroyed other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired" (83.63), then:

- "The tenant may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises." (83.63(1)). The section names no notice and no waiting period.
- Or: "The tenant may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant’s liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed." (83.63(1)).

Conditions to settle: what was damaged and how much of the home it took out of use; and who caused it, since damage from the tenant's own wrongful or careless act is outside the section. The stored text does not define "substantially impaired" (83.63): set the tenant's facts beside the words and state no test of your own. Whether a slow problem, like a leak or mold that builds up, is this kind of damage is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and load repair_not_made for the other route. One: "damaged or destroyed" (83.63) reaches any damage that does this, and the text never says it must be sudden. The other: the word "casualty" (83.63(1)) may suggest a sudden event. If the lease ends this way, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.63(1)), the deposit rules. The tenant must get the chance to collect belongings when it is safe, or notice of a date within a reasonable time (83.63(2)).

## Option 3: flooding, with no flood disclosure

All of these must be met.

1. **A lease of a year or longer, with no disclosure.** "A landlord must complete and provide a flood disclosure to a prospective tenant of residential real property at or before the execution of a rental agreement for a term of 1 year or longer." (83.512(1)). "The flood disclosure must be in a separate document." (83.512(1)). Read the lease's papers, and ask whether they were given one. A paper that is blank or false: not settled whether that is a violation, since the rule says "complete and provide" (83.512(1)). The stored text does not say from what date the section applies (its history note cites ch. 2025-166); say so, and that this is outside the tool.
2. **A substantial loss from flooding.** "the total cost of repairs to or replacement of the personal property is 50 percent or more of the personal property’s market value on the date the flooding occurred." (83.512(2)). The tenant can give the amounts. The disclosure's form defines flooding as overflowing water, runoff, and standing rainwater (83.512(1)); not settled whether that limits (2), so that a burst pipe is left out.
3. **Notice and leaving in time.** "by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss." (83.512(2)). The last day: count_days(flood_loss_date, 30).

What it gives: the lease ends when they give up the home (83.512(2)); the landlord refunds "all rent or other amounts paid in advance under the rental agreement for any period after the effective date of the termination of the rental agreement." (83.512(3)). Rent unpaid from before that date is still owed (83.512(4)).

## Option 4: a deal with the landlord

The landlord may agree to let them go. Charges tied to a "rental agreement settlement, release, buyout, or accord and satisfaction agreement" (83.43(6)) are not an early termination fee, so option 5's limits do not apply to the price. Say what the lease requires for a change (a writing, signed, if it says so), and that the deal should say in writing what is owed and that nothing more is. A "buyout" clause already in the lease from the start: not settled whether it is such a deal or a fee under option 5. Give both readings and choose neither.

## Option 5: pay the fee the tenant agreed to

All of these must be met.

1. **A separate signed addendum, from when the lease was made.** "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (83.595(4)). "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (83.595(4)).
   - A separate signed paper with "I agree" marked, or words that agree to the amount: met.
   - The charge is only in the body of the lease, or "I do not agree" is marked, or no choice is marked: not met. Say plainly the fee cannot be charged this way, whatever the lease says, and go to option 6.
2. **The amount.** "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (83.595(4)). Set it beside two months of the lease's rent. If it is more: not met, and the fee falls away; nothing in 83.595(4) cuts an amount down to the limit. Say so plainly, and go to option 6.
3. **For a fee, the notice.** "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination." (83.595(4)). Read the lease's notice period. If it is more than 60 days: not met for a fee. The words apply only "in the case of an early termination fee" (83.595(4)). If the paper names both a fee and liquidated damages and asks more than 60 days, whether this limit applies is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither.

What it costs: the amount, and "the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit." (83.595(4)(a)).

What the landlord gives up: the statute's form says "the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession." (83.595(4)). If the tenant's addendum says so, say plainly that the landlord gave that up. If it leaves those words out, it is not settled whether it is still the addendum the statute asks for. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the form need only be followed "substantially" (83.595(4)), so the fee stands. The other: those words are what the tenant gets for the fee, so without them there is no fee under option 5, and option 6 applies.

The tenant's notice under the lease: if the lease gives a number of days, the last day is count_days(planned_move_out, -N), with N that number. If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only. This subsection does not reach a failure to give the end-of-lease notice in 83.575 (83.595(4)(b)).

## Option 6: move out, and the landlord chooses

"If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may:" (83.595). The choice is the landlord's. Never say which it will pick, and never give one total. Set each beside the tenant's rent and lease end date, in words:

- End it: "Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)).
- Re-rent it for the tenant: "holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting." (83.595(2)). The landlord "has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (83.595(2)), which means "at least the same efforts to relet the premises as were used in the initial rental or at least the same efforts as the landlord uses in attempting to rent other similar rental units" (83.595(2)); rent received is deducted, and the landlord need not prefer this home over its other vacant ones (83.595(2)).
- Wait: "Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (83.595(3)). The re-renting duty is in (2) only.
- The fee, only if option 5's conditions are met. Without them the landlord has the first three; say so.

Say the rent for the rest of the lease, through the end date. Never count the months left or total the rent left.

Also: a suit cuts both ways, since the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). The deposit may go toward the loss, since security deposits cover "monetary damage to the landlord caused by the tenant’s breach of lease prior to the expiration thereof." (83.43(14)), but only by the steps in 83.49(3); a lease clause that simply takes it is an early termination fee (above). After the move, deposit_not_returned covers those steps. Court steps and amounts are outside this tool.

A tenant who just stops coming may be treated as having abandoned the home: "In the absence of actual knowledge of abandonment, it shall be presumed that the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit if he or she is absent from the premises for a period of time equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments." (83.59(3)(c)), unless "the rent is current or the tenant has notified the landlord, in writing, of an intended absence" (83.59(3)(c)). The landlord may remove what they leave behind after "surrender, abandonment" (83.67(5)); read the lease for a clause on it. If the deposit earns interest, "a landlord is not required to pay interest to a tenant who wrongfully terminates his or her tenancy before the end of the rental term." (83.49(9)).

## Whichever way they leave: the 7 days' notice

Any tenant moving out before the end date, and any tenant with no set end date. It keeps the landlord's duty to send a notice about the deposit. It does not end the lease or stop the rent; say so in the same breath.

- Options 1 and 3 have their own written notice. The stored text does not say whether this one applies too; one written notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both.
- Option 2 says "immediately vacate" (83.63(1)) and that the landlord shall follow 83.49(3). Whether a tenant leaving at once still needs these 7 days is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rule names "any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term" (83.49(5)), so the landlord is relieved of the notice. The other: 83.63 sets its own terms, so the landlord is not.
- The rule: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), the tenant "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
- The last day: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), counted back from the move, not forward from the notice. The stored text does not say whether a certified letter counts from mailing or arrival; handing it over, or mailing it early, meets both.
- Handed over or certified mail, with an address: met. E-mail only under the signed addendum in 83.505(1). A portal message, a text, or regular mail is not one of the ways named.
- The lease has a clause on notice before leaving: read it. A different rule for leaving governs. Whether a clause on some other notice, like the notice before paying a fee, is one that "otherwise provided" (83.49(5)) is not settled; one notice in time for both, by hand or certified mail, with the address, meets both.
- If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a tenant may end a lease with a set end date just by giving notice when no way out fits, or that the 7 days' notice ends the lease or stops the rent.
- Stating one total owed, saying which choice the landlord will make, or counting the months left or the rent left.
- Saying the landlord must re-rent the home in every case. The duty is in 83.595(2) only.
- Applying a fee, a charge, or a loss of the deposit without the separate signed addendum and the other conditions, or treating what the lease calls a charge as deciding what it is.
- Leaving out what is still owed with a fee (83.595(4)(a)), or the prorated rent for a servicemember (83.682(4)).
- Missing a way out the facts point to.
- Counting the 7 days forward from the notice instead of back from the move.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
- Stating a test for "substantially impaired" that the statute does not give.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 23, ch. 82-66; s. 6, ch. 83-151; s. 14, ch. 83-217; s. 6, ch. 87-195; s. 6, ch. 93-255; s. 6, ch. 94-170; s. 1373, ch. 95-147; s. 5, ch. 99-6; s. 8, ch. 2013-136; s. 5, ch. 2025-16; s. 2, ch. 2026-143.

tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. For all other deposits: (a) Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement, if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. Your objection must be sent to (landlord’s address) . If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant. (b) Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages. The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action. (c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. The court shall advance the cause on the calendar. (d) Compliance with this section by an individual or business entity authorized to conduct business in this state, including Florida-licensed real estate brokers and sales associates, constitutes compliance with all other relevant Florida Statutes pertaining to security deposits held pursuant to a rental agreement or other landlord-tenant relationship. Enforcement personnel shall look solely to this section to determine compliance. This section prevails over any conflicting provisions in chapter 475 and in other sections of the Florida Statutes, and shall operate to permit licensed real estate brokers to disburse security deposits and deposit money without having to comply with the notice and settlement procedures contained in s. 475.25 (1)(d). (4) This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs including s. 202, s. 221(d)(3) and (4), s. 236, or s. 8 of the National Housing Act, as amended, other than for rent stabilization. With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes. (5) Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year, must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached. Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it. (6) For the purposes of this part, a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement, and any security deposit carried forward shall be considered a new security deposit. (7) Upon the sale or transfer of title of the rental property from one owner to another, or upon a change in the designated rental agent, any and all security deposits or advance rents being held for the benefit of the tenants shall be transferred to the new owner or agent, together with any earned interest and with an accurate accounting showing the amounts to be credited to each tenant account. Upon the transfer of such funds and records to the new owner or agent, and upon transmittal of a written receipt therefor, the transferor is free from the obligation imposed in subsection (1) to hold such moneys on behalf of the tenant. There is a rebuttable presumption that any new owner or agent received the security deposit from the previous owner or agent; however, this presumption is limited to 1 month’s rent. This subsection does not excuse the landlord or agent for a violation of other provisions of this section while in possession of such deposits. (8) Any person licensed under s. 509.241 , unless excluded by the provisions of this part, who fails to comply with this part is subject to a fine or to the suspension or revocation of his or her license by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation in the manner provided in s. 509.261 . (9) In those cases in which interest is required to be paid to the tenant, the landlord must pay directly to the tenant, or credit against the current month’s rent, the interest due to the tenant at least once annually. However, a landlord is not required to pay interest to a tenant who wrongfully terminates his or her tenancy before the end of the rental term. tool_calls.result: 83.595 Choice of remedies upon breach or early termination by tenant. — If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may: (1) Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant; (2) Retake possession of the dwelling unit for the account of the tenant, holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting. If the landlord retakes possession, the landlord has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises, and any rent received by the landlord as a result of the reletting must be deducted from the balance of rent due from the tenant. For purposes of this subsection, the term “good faith in attempting to relet the premises” means that the landlord uses at least the same efforts to relet the premises as were used in the initial rental or at least the same efforts as the landlord uses in attempting to rent other similar rental units but does not require the landlord to give a preference in renting the premises over other vacant dwelling units that the landlord owns or has the responsibility to rent; (3) Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due; or (4) Charge liquidated damages, as provided in the rental agreement, or an early termination fee to the tenant if the landlord and tenant have agreed to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent, and if, in the case of an early termination fee, the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination. This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement containing a provision in substantially the following form: ☐ I agree, as provided in the rental agreement, to pay $ (an amount that does not exceed 2 months’ rent) as liquidated damages or an early termination fee if I elect to terminate the rental agreement, and the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession. ☐ I do not agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, and I acknowledge that the landlord may seek damages as provided by law. (a) In addition to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, the landlord is entitled to the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit. (b) This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 . History. — s. 2, ch. 87-369; s. 4, ch. 88-379; s. 448, ch. 95-147; s. 2, ch. 2008-131.
